name: Eastern Mnong
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: In this paper, we focus on a dialect of Eastern Mnong, Râlâm spoken in the commune of Yang Tao, in the district of Lăk, in Đắk Lắk province, Vietnam. ... Target words were either monosyllables or sesquisyllables ending in target syllables. Sequisyllables are disyllables in which the final stressed syllable has the full array of contrasts while the initial syllable, or presyllable, has a reduced inventory (Thomas 1992).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Eastern Mnong (east2333) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Simpson 1999 'accents in pop and rock singing' (Multilingua), is a Glottolog keyword-pollution hit ('pop'/'lam') about English singing accents and has no bearing on Mnong; paywalled, no abstract available, priority none. Going beyond the list of works with stress in the title, I downloaded the open SEAlang Mon-Khmer Studies holdings on Mnong (Blood 1976 phonemes of Rơlơm; Blood & Blood 1966, 1969; Phillips 1973 x2) to and scanned the two phonological ones. Blood 1976, the first-hand Eastern Mnong (Rơlơm) phonology, is silent on word stress (only a vowel-shortness prosodic feature and an I C (T) syllable pattern). Phillips 1973 mentions 'the main stressed syllable' (p. 120) but is expressly about Central Mnong and excludes Rơlơm. No first-hand Eastern Mnong stress statement was obtained (no new stress statement was found). Highest-value unreached items for this language: Blood 1963 MA thesis 'The vowel system of Uon Njuñ Mnong Rơlơm' (Indiana), Blood, Blood & Hmok 1976 Mnong Rơlơm dictionary and Hmok 1976 Mnong Lam language lessons (SIL Vietnam; old sil.org repository links dead), and Vietnamese-language grammars/dictionaries (e.g. Nguyễn Kiên Trường & Trương Anh 2009 Từ điển Việt-M'Nông). written in the save directory.

(Sequisyllables italic, Thomas 1992 a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in a sesquisyllable the final (main) syllable is the stressed one and the initial presyllable is reduced. This is a definitional sentence (attributed to Thomas 1992, a Bunong/Central Mnong thesis) applied to the authors' Râlâm stimulus words, not an explicit stress rule for the language.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. Supporting but non-specific: Sidwell 2000: 40 says South Bahnaric minor syllables 'are always unstressed'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (isolated stimulus words in a carrier frame); Râlâm of Yang Tao commune, Lăk district, Đắk Lắk. The primary phonemic description of the same variety (Blood 1976) is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand material is for the Rơlơm/Râlâm/Rlăm dialect of Eastern Mnong (Lăk / Lac Thiện district, Đắk Lắk): Blood 1976 = Uon Njuñ sub-dialect; Brunelle et al. 2025 = Yang Tao commune, said to be nearly identical to the Njuñ and Lê varieties. Glottolog east2333 lists no dialect children; 'Rolom' is an alternate name of east2333. Phillips 1973 (both papers) and Butler 2015 describe Central Mnong (Bunong, ISO cmo), not this language.

tone_statements.citation: Brunelle, Marc, Đinh Lư Giang & Tạ Thành Tấn. 2025. Redundant voicing and register in Mnong Râlâm. Phonetica 82(1): 45-85. doi:10.1515/phon-2024-0023
tone_statements.quote: In this paper, we present acoustic and perceptual evidence that an Eastern Mnong variety, Râlâm, has a form of register, contrary to expectations, and show that this register is largely redundant with onset voicing. ... Despite its robustness, Mnong Râlâm obstruent voicing is redundant with a well-developed register system that is largely realized through F1 modulations resulting in a weak ongliding at the beginning of vowels. ... As for f0, it is at best a negligible property in the Mnong Râlâm register contrast (especially in dentals)
tone_statements.locator: §1 Introduction (opening paragraph) and §4 Discussion and conclusion (2nd paragraph); PMC HTML, pages not marked
tone_statements.summary: Two-way register contrast (high/low), redundant with onset stop voicing, cued mainly by F1; f0 negligible. Authors treat register as distinct from tone; no lexical tone described.

sources.citation: Blood, Henry F. (1976). The phonemes of Uon Njuñ Mnong Rơlơm. Mon-Khmer Studies 5: 4-23.
sources.quote: 5.4 Prosodic Feature. Uon Njuñ Mnong Rơlơm has a shortness feature which occurs as a distinctive feature only with the vowels /i o a u/ and only in closed syllables (syllables having termination). This feature also occurs redundantly on /v/ which is always short (occurring only in closed syllables) and on /o/ in closed syllables. [...] 6.1 Mnong Rơlơm Syllable Pattern. Mnong Rơlơm syllable pattern may be represented by I C (T), in which I (Initiation) and C (Culmination) are obligatory and T (Termination) is optional.
sources.note: First-hand phonology of the Rơlơm dialect (= Eastern Mnong per Glottolog alt. name 'Rolom'), read in full via scanned (no text; tesseract 300 dpi). It is SILENT on stress: no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' or 'presyllable' anywhere in the 20 pages. The only prosodic statement is a vowel-shortness feature (sec. 5.4, p. 15) and the syllable pattern I C (T) (sec. 6.1, p. 16); words are treated at the syllable level only, so no polysyllabic stress rule is given.
sources.venue: Mon-Khmer Studies: A Journal of Southeast Asian Linguistics and Languages 5

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2000. Proto South Bahnaric: a reconstruction of a Mon-Khmer language of Indo-China. Pacific Linguistics 501. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Comparative work; §1.2.1 gives the Bahnaric word template (minor syllable + main syllable) and p. 40 (§3.1.3) states minorsyllables 'are always unstressed, and can be dropped in speech if it does not cause ambiguity' — a general South Bahnaric statement based on Chrau, Stieng, Koho (Mnong only via Blood 1966's lexicon), not specific to Eastern Mnong.

tone.quote: In Fig. 4, we see that mean f0 is higher in the high than the low register at vowel onset. However, this effect is weak: it is not significant after coronals (RegisterLow: β = -9.6, t = -0.91, p = 0.42) but is after velars .. Contrary to our expectations and to previous descriptions, Mnong Râlâm already seems to have a well-developed register system largely based on vowel quality and phonation (RQ2). .. We conclude that Mnong Râlâm has a stable register system that is reinforced by optional closure voicing (especially in men). It is likely that previous researchers described it as a language with a voicing contrast in onset stops because of this frequent secondary closure voicing.
